title: Davis-Bacon Apprenticeship Ratio Requirements: What Contractors Must Track on Federally Funded Projects
summary: How apprentice-to-journeyman ratios work on Davis-Bacon projects, what must appear on certified payroll, and what happens when ratios are violated.
body_markdown:
Apprentices can reduce labor costs on a Davis-Bacon project, but only if every classification, wage rate, and ratio requirement is handled correctly. One apprentice over the allowable ratio, one unregistered worker classified as an apprentice, or one missed wage step advancement can turn a routine certified payroll review into back wages, penalties, and an audit finding that follows the contractor to the next bid.


Ratios vary by trade, by state, and by the specific apprenticeship program under which each worker is registered. For back-office administrators and compliance leads on federally funded projects, understanding how ratios are set, how violations are triggered, and how apprentice classification must appear on ​[certified payroll reports](https://www.buildtrayd.com/solution/compliance/certified-payroll) is a core compliance obligation.


## **What an Apprenticeship Ratio Requirement Actually Controls**


An apprentice-to-journeyman ratio determines how many apprentice hours or apprentice workers can be present on a jobsite relative to the number of journeyworkers performing the same trade. The ratio exists to ensure apprentices receive adequate supervision and training while preventing contractors from staffing projects disproportionately with lower-paid apprentice labor.


Under the Davis-Bacon Act, apprentices may be paid less than the journeyman prevailing wage rate only if two conditions are met simultaneously. First, the apprentice must be individually registered in a bona fide apprenticeship program registered with the[U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Apprenticeship (OA)](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/apprenticeship) or a State Apprenticeship Agency recognized by OA. Second, the number of apprentices on the jobsite must fall within the ratio established by that apprenticeship program's approved standards.


If either condition fails, the apprentice must be paid the full journeyman prevailing wage rate for all hours worked. According to the[DOL's DBRA Compliance Principles guidance](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/government-contracts/prevailing-wage-resource-book/db-compliance-principles) , unregistered workers, sometimes called "pre-apprentices," are not recognized under Davis-Bacon and cannot be paid a reduced rate.


## **How Apprentice-to-Journeyman Ratios Are Set Per Trade**


Ratios are not established by the Davis-Bacon Act itself. Each approved apprenticeship program defines its own ratio requirements in its program standards, which are reviewed and approved by the DOL Office of Apprenticeship or the applicable State Apprenticeship Agency.


### **Where the Ratios Come From**


The ratio published in the apprenticeship program standards is the one that applies on a Davis-Bacon project, not the ratio that may appear in a collective bargaining agreement. A contractor performing electrical work under a program with a 3:1 ratio, as cited in DOL compliance training materials, must have at least three journey-level electricians on the jobsite for every one apprentice electrician.


Because ratios are program-specific, contractors working multiple trades on the same project may need to track different ratios simultaneously. A ​[pre-bid compliance checklist](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/pre-bid-compliance-checklist-public-works-contractors) should confirm the applicable ratio for every trade that will have apprentices on site before work begins.


### **Two Critical Enforcement Rules**


The DOL applies two rules that catch contractors off guard:


-


**Ratios are enforced per jobsite, not across the contractor's workforce.** A contractor cannot average the ratio across multiple projects. If the program standards require a 3:1 ratio, that ratio must be met at each individual worksite where apprentices are performing work.


-


**Ratios are calculated daily, not weekly.** If a journeyworker calls out sick on a Tuesday and the remaining crew composition falls below the required ratio for that day, the apprentice hours worked on Tuesday may be out of compliance. Averaging hours across the week does not correct a daily ratio violation.


## **What Happens When a Ratio Is Violated Mid-Project**


A ratio violation does not shut down the jobsite, but the financial consequences are immediate and retroactive.


### **Pay Consequences**


All apprentice hours worked in excess of the allowable ratio must be paid at the full journeyman prevailing wage rate for the classification of work performed. The contractor cannot apply the reduced apprentice rate to those hours, even if the apprentice is otherwise properly registered and enrolled in an approved program. The overage is calculated based on the ratio that should have applied on the specific day the violation occurred.


A ratio violation that goes undetected across several pay periods can generate significant back wage liability by the time a certified payroll audit surfaces the issue.


### **Audit and Enforcement Exposure**


Ratio violations surface during certified payroll reviews conducted by contracting agencies and the[DOL Wage and Hour Division](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd) . Documented enforcement actions include cases where contractors were placed on the ineligible bidders list for employing apprentices in excess of the allowed ratio, as reported by the[Government Accountability Office](https://www.gao.gov/) . Debarment from federal contracts for up to three years remains a possible consequence.


## **How Apprenticeship Classification Shows Up on Certified Payroll Reports**


Apprentice classification on the WH-347 or equivalent certified payroll form must reflect the worker's actual registration status, wage step, and applicable rate. A ​[certified payroll guide](https://www.buildtrayd.com/blog/certified-payroll-guide-2026) that covers apprentice documentation should be part of every compliance lead's reference library.


### **Required Documentation Elements**


Each apprentice listed on a certified payroll report must include:


-


**Registration status:** The worker must be individually registered in a DOL or state-approved apprenticeship program. The program name and registration number should be available for verification.


-


**Wage rate expressed as a percentage of the journeyman rate.** Apprentice pay is calculated as a percentage of the journeyman hourly rate, based on the apprentice's current progress step in the program. A first-year electrical apprentice at 50% of the journeyman rate earns a different hourly amount than a third-year apprentice at 75%.


-


**Fringe benefit obligations.** Apprentices on Davis-Bacon projects are entitled to fringe benefits as specified in the apprenticeship agreement. The fringe amount must appear on the certified payroll alongside the base hourly rate.


-


**Classification alignment.** The work classification listed on the certified payroll must match the trade for which the apprentice is registered. An apprentice registered in an electrical program who performs plumbing work must be paid the journeyman plumbing rate for those hours.


## **Common Apprenticeship Ratio Tracking Mistakes**


Compliance teams managing apprentice ratios across active projects should watch for five recurring errors that generate audit findings and back wage exposure.


### **Mistakes That Trigger Violations**


-


**Assuming ratios are the same across all trades and states.** A ratio that works for one trade in one jurisdiction may not apply to a different trade or a different state's apprenticeship program. Each program's approved standards control.


-


**Averaging ratios over the week instead of tracking daily.** Most agencies enforce ratios based on daily presence and supervision. A contractor who meets the ratio on a weekly average but violates it on individual days is still out of compliance.


-


**Counting supervisors or foremen who are not performing journeyman work.** Only journey-level workers actively performing the same trade classification count toward the ratio. A superintendent walking the site does not satisfy the journeyman count for the electrical crew's ratio.


-


**Paying the same apprentice wage step for the duration of the project.** Apprentice wage rates are tied to program milestones. When an apprentice advances to the next step mid-project, the ​[payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll) rate must be updated accordingly. Failing to advance the rate results in underpayment.


-


**Not retaining apprenticeship documentation.** Program registration records, apprenticeship agreements, and wage step verification must be kept on file. Missing documentation during an audit can invalidate the apprentice classification entirely.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### What is the apprenticeship ratio requirement on a prevailing wage project?


The ratio determines how many apprentices can work relative to journeyworkers in the same trade on a jobsite. Ratios are set by each apprenticeship program's approved standards, not by a single federal number, and vary by trade, state, and program.


### How do I track apprentice-to-journeyman ratios for certified payroll?


Track the ratio daily at each jobsite by counting journey-level workers actively performing each trade against the number of apprentices in that trade. Compare the count to the ratio published in the applicable apprenticeship program standards.


### What happens if an apprentice exceeds the allowed ratio?


All apprentice hours worked in excess of the allowable ratio must be paid at the full journeyman prevailing wage rate. The contractor cannot apply the reduced apprentice rate to those excess hours.


### Can an unregistered worker be classified as an apprentice on a Davis-Bacon project?


No. Only workers individually registered in a program approved by the DOL Office of Apprenticeship or a recognized State Apprenticeship Agency qualify for apprentice classification. Unregistered workers must be paid the full journeyman rate.


### Are apprenticeship ratios calculated daily or weekly?


Ratios are enforced on a daily basis at each individual jobsite. Weekly averaging does not satisfy the requirement, and a single day out of ratio can constitute a violation.


### Do apprentice fringe benefits need to appear on the certified payroll report?


Yes. Apprentices on Davis-Bacon projects are entitled to fringe benefits as specified in the apprenticeship agreement. The fringe amount must be documented on the certified payroll alongside the base hourly rate.
